after: ## The five methods at a glance
alt: Five rows, each with a small icon: narration (a time line), cause-effect (a chain of boxes), comparison-contrast (two boxes side by side), definition (a boundary around a term) and description (an eye). Each lists what the method does, its signal words and the question it answers.
caption: Narration, cause-effect, comparison-contrast, definition, description: each helps readers trace the reasoning.

after: ## The same topic developed five ways
alt: The old reading room sits at the centre with five developments around it: narration (Zainab’s visit), cause-effect (cut hours leading to the homework club halving), comparison-contrast (Harbourside’s hours and spending), definition (a public place “without paying”) and description (radiator dust and green lamps).
caption: The same thesis can be developed five ways; each shapes what the reader feels.

alt: Five needs mapped to methods: make a point human (narration), show why it matters (cause-effect), show one option is better (comparison-contrast), fix a term’s meaning (definition), help the audience see a situation (description). Audience, purpose and length also shape the choice.
caption: Choose the method that does the job the argument needs at that point.

alt: Three panels show a dominant method containing others: narration with description and cause-effect reflection; definition with a comparison (“A library is unlike a shop because...”); cause-effect with a narrative example.
caption: One method usually dominates a paragraph while others work inside it.

alt: Four story steps: a ship lost at sea signals for water; the reply is “Cast down your bucket where you are”; puzzled, they ask again; they lower the bucket and draw fresh water at the mouth of a river. Below, the analogy maps the ship to the Southern community and the water to opportunity and cooperation close at hand.
caption: Narration can carry an argument by analogy, letting the audience reach the conclusion.

alt: Four passages matched to their dominant method with the signal that shows it: the bridge closure is cause-effect (“so”), the two schools side by side is comparison-contrast, “By ‘fairness’ I do not mean...” is definition, and the fishing trip in June is narration.
caption: Each identification cites a signal in the text; one method dominates each passage.

after: ## Worked example 2: choosing and applying a method
alt: A three-step plan for persuading a sceptical headteacher: open with cause-effect (the survey of Monday exhaustion), then comparison-contrast (a neighbouring school that has tried the policy), then narration (the Year 9 pupil’s lost Sunday) to give the case a human face.
caption: Audience, purpose and evidence decide which method comes first.
